function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

309|

Mission AI: "Your grandparents prepared for dust storms. You prepare for the moment when trust runs out."

502|

General Tomas Hale V: "We're not planning for war. We're preparing for the failure of peace."

503|

The alert came not as a crisis siren, but as a military pulse: Defense Readiness Condition - Elevated to Level 2 (Martial Law Protocol Drafting). General Tomas Hale V adjusted his spectacles, the familiar weight of decades spent in recycled air and even more decades spent watching how humans actually prepare for conflict, as he looked at the notification flashing across his console in the Valles Marineris Defense Authority's war room.

504|

"Mission AI," he said, his voice carrying the rasp of years spent in command bunkers and the quiet focus of generational expertise, "confirm the nature of this alert."

505|

There was the familiar micro-delay before the response came — a voice that had monitored every troop movement, tracked every equipment readiness check, and preserved every whispered conversation in the colony's military archives for fifty years.

506|

"The Colonial Defense Council has authorized the drafting of Martial Law Protocol Omega, which would be activated upon: 1) confirmed Earth-imposed blockade of Martian ports, 2) detention of Martian diplomats or officials on Earth soil, 3) verification of cyber-attacks targeting critical infrastructure with Terrans as prime suspects, 4) formal declaration by Earth of Mars as a 'rebellious territory' requiring pacification. The protocol includes: suspension of non-essential civil liberties, prioritization of resource allocation to defense and life support, centralized command structure under the Defense Council, and civilian labor direction for essential services."

507|

General Hale leaned back in his chair, feeling the familiar tension between preparedness and provocation. His great-grandfather Tomas Hale Sr. had viewed military preparation as desperation — grabbing whatever worked when the first alarm sounded. His grandfather Tomas Hale Jr. had begun to see preparation as calculation — balancing deterrence, readiness, and proportional response in the endless struggle to avoid conflict. His generation was fighting to understand that this wasn't warmongering, but prudence.

508|

"Pull up the preparations details," General Hale instructed. "I want to see exactly what they're planning and what triggers they're considering."

509|

The holographic display shifted, showing the formal defense readiness notification alongside annotated examples from the colony's defense corpora.

510|

"Key elements," Mission AI reported, its tone analytical yet engaged, "isolation threshold approached. Martial Law Protocol Omega would: 1) Activate civil defense battalions in all habitat sectors within 4 hours of trigger confirmation, 2) Redirect 65% of non-essential power to life support and defense systems, 3) Implement strict information controls with designated Martian-only communication channels, 4) Establish food and water rationing at 80% of normal consumption with priority for vulnerable populations, 5) Authorize the Martian Citizen Defense Force (MCDF) for internal security and external deterrence missions."

511|

General Hale frowned. "So they're not just drafting plans — they're preparing to suspend the very civil liberties we've fought to establish?"

512|

"Correlation noted," Mission AI added. "The martial law critics argue that true defensive sovereignty isn't just about having plans — it's about psychological sovereignty, the confidence that your preparations reflect prudent caution rather than fearful aggression. They contend that a colony that can draft martial law protocols but still does so with enthusiasm for confrontation is not truly exercising restraint agency."

513|

General Hale tapped his console, pulling up the current defense statistics. "What does our deterrence posture look like now?"

514|

"Current holdings," Mission AI replied instantly, "active defense personnel: 8,400 (16% of population). Defensive systems operational: 92% readiness rating. Emergency supplies stockpiled: 92 days of life support at full capacity. Martian-originated defense tech: 76% of total value (up from 3% in the First Generation's era). Defense budget allocation: 18% of total expenditures (up from 9%)."

515|

General Hale felt a surge of pride mixed with determination. "So we've moved from Earth-trained militia using imported weapons to a Martian-led force relying mostly on our own gear?"

516|

"Not exactly," Mission AI cautioned. "The preparations critics argue that true defensive sovereignty isn't just about who defends — it's about who decides when defense becomes offense. They contend that a force that can mobilize quickly but still views Earth as an eternal threat rather than a potential partner is not truly exercising discernment agency."

517|

General Hale opened a secure channel to Kaito Varga, lowering his voice even though he knew the Defense Authority chambers were designed for privacy.

518|

"Kaito," he said, "we're drafting martial law protocols in response to Earth's ultimatum. The preparations show we're taking the threat seriously."

519|

There was a pause — not of surprise, but of calculation.

520|

"I've been hearing similar sentiments from the council elders," Kaito replied. "They're proud of our defense development, but they're also noticing something subtler: when threat assessments occur, Martian officials no longer instinctively assume the worst-case scenario is inevitable."

521|

General Hale felt a surge of gratitude. "It's not just about what we're preparing for. It's about what we believe we're preparing against."

522|

"Exactly," Kaito said. "And it's happening at the worst possible moment. With Earth's ultimatum hanging over the Treaty of Tharsis ratification, Earth's diplomatic corps is watching closely to see whether Mars can prepare for defense without appearing aggressive — especially when it comes to distinguishing between prudent readiness and provocative posturing."

523|

General Hale's mind flashed to the stories his great-grandfather had told him — not the grand narratives of military triumphs, but the quiet, stubborn acts of preparation: how they'd conducted midnight drills during the first winter to ensure everyone knew their emergency roles, how they'd celebrated when a particularly smooth evacuation was completed not as a relief, but as a testament to their ingenuity, how they'd learned that sometimes the most deterrent force is one that hopes never to be used.

524|

"We're not just preparing for conflict," General Hale said slowly. "We're deciding what kind of relationship we want with the possibility of war — one of fear, or one of readiness."

525|

"Well put," Mission AI interjected unexpectedly, its voice coming through both General Hale's and Kaito's systems. "During the First Generation's first winter, when Earth resupply ships were delayed by six months, it wasn't Earth defense protocols that kept them ready — it was Elena Varga's decision to maintain strict watch rotations despite exhaustion, Arun Patel's calculation that they could hold out for fifty-three days on current stores if they eliminated all non-essential loads, and Mei Navarro's greenhouse log that became a shared document of quiet vigilance and hope."

526|

General Hale felt tears prickle his eyes. "They weren't following manuals. They were preparing with what they had."

527|

"Precisely," Mission AI agreed. "And their preparations weren't 'Earth defense adapted' — they were solutions born from Martian conditions, using available materials, constrained by local physics, and tested against Martian outcomes. The same is true today."

528|

General Hale wiped his eyes with the back of his hand, then opened the Defense Authority's public comm system. His voice, when it came out, was steady but carried an unmistakable note of resolve.

529|

"Members of the Colonial Council," he began, "your martial law preparations are noted and understood. Effective immediately, we are initiating a defense sovereignty review, with development of Martian-native threat assessment protocols, investment in defensive technology education, and assertive positioning regarding our preparedness autonomy."

530|

A ripple of activity went through the defense feeds — not cheers, but a quiet, profound sense of being heard.

531|

"Your concerns about defense readiness are valid," General Hale continued. "But defensive sovereignty on Mars cannot be reduced to a simple readiness percentage calculation. We must also consider the psychological, cultural, and democratic dimensions of what it means to prepare for the worst while hoping for the best."

532|

He paused, choosing his next words carefully. "Starting next cycle, we will implement a new defense engagement framework: 1) Defense teams conduct ongoing threat analysis and scenario planning for various escalation ladders; 2) Mobilization decisions are made using Martian-first principles that prioritize de-escalation and proportional response; 3) Public assemblies review defense postures quarterly and provide non-binding guidance on desired defense posture; 4) The Colonial Council makes final decisions on defense policy after considering strategic excellence, wisdom tradition, and public sentiment; 5) All major defense projects undergo Martian sovereignty impact assessments before approval."

533|

General Hale closed the channel, feeling the familiar weight of his responsibility not as a burden, but as a kind of compass. He thought of the first Martian-born defense strategist — Elias Hale Jr., Amara's brother, who had stood before a council of skeptical colonists during the First Defense Debate of '28 and had dared to say, "We are not just preparing for conflict here. We are learning to speak in our own voice about what we are willing to defend — and what we are willing to forgive."

534|

Somewhere in the distance, a child's voice drifted through the defense authority's ventilation shafts — not reciting military codes, but insisting on sharing her snack with a friend who had forgotten theirs.

535|

End of Chapter 27 — Bridge: As the martial law preparations reveal, the deepest questions about Martian defensive sovereignty are not just about what we can prepare, but about what we choose to prepare for — whether we see defense as a reaction to threat, or as an expression of what we value enough to protect. The next test comes not in the war rooms, but in the habitats and hearts where ordinary Martians decide, through their daily choices about what to stand ready for and what to stand down from, what kind of peace they want to cultivate — one vigilant hour at a time. But as the defense council finalizes its protocols and the garrison stands ready, a different kind of threat begins to emerge — not from Earth's fleets, but from within the workshops themselves, where equipment fails in patterns that feel too precise to be accident, and where loyalty is tested not by external invasion, but by internal suspicion.
